newsitem.title: USA: Intel sees continued PC shipment growth.
newsitem.headline: Intel sees continued PC shipment growth.

text.p: Intel Corp. Senior Vice President Albert Yu said on Thursday that worldwide personal computer shipment growth rates are likely to continue to grow at levels of 18-19 percent this year.

"It seems reasonable," that global PC shipment rates will continue to grow at the historic 18-19 percent levels that independent research groups have forecast will continue, Yu told reporters after a presentation to investors here.
"The growth rate of the emerging markets is absolutely phenomenal," he said earlier in his presentation to a Hambrecht & Quist technology conference here.

Yu, who heads Intel's Microprocessor Group, also said in response to a reporter's question afterwards that shipments of its new Pentium II processor, which it is due to formally unveil next week, could outpace sales of its high-end Pentium Pro chips by the end of this year.

Yu said the market acceptance of the company's MMX multimedia technology, which adds instructions that support improved audiovisual capabilities, has exceeded that of any other previous processor technology.
MMX was introduced on some of Intel's Pentium chip family in January this year, and by the first quarter of 1998 he said it would be on all its microprocessors.

Yu did not make projections of his own for personal computer growth, but he noted the industry's growth rate has tracked the 18 to 19 percent range worldwide and was "forecast to be in that range in the foreseeable future" by industry research groups.

The executive noted that the North and South America share of the market has declined to around 40 percent last year from some 60 percent in 1986 as Europe remained in the 26-27 percent range and Asia markets grew their share of shipments dramatically.
"Now it is really a global market and everyone around the world is using PCs in really a dramatic fashion," he said in his presentation.
In Intel's move to produce "faster, cheaper, better" products, the company expects to continue to produce dramatic increases in processor performance.
Yu repeated Intel's projection that by the year 2011 it should be able to put one billion transistors on a microprocessor, compared with 5.5 million today.
The company said this factor of 200 increase in the number of transistors will translate into even greater growth in microprocessor performance.
While leading chips today can process 300 million instructions per second (MIPS), a common measure of computing performance, by the year 2011 a process should run at 100,000 MIPS.

He noted this was similar to the performance growth rate over the last 10 to 15 years. "The chances are very good that we can continue at this rate," he said. (sam.perry@reuters.com, Palo Alto Bureau 415 846 5400)
